title: Anticoagulated Head Injury: Acute Subdural Hematoma
description: Scan within the hour when risk factors appear, reverse warfarin with prothrombin complex concentrate, and decide on evacuation using the subdural hematoma surgical criteria.
objectives: Apply NICE criteria for the timing of a head CT
Reverse warfarin with prothrombin complex concentrate, not plasma
Use hematoma thickness, midline shift, GCS trajectory, pupils, and ICP to decide on evacuation
Know what RESCUE-ASDH showed about craniotomy versus craniectomy

references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Head injury: assessment and early management. NICE guideline NG232. London: NICE; 2023.
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Blood transfusion. NICE guideline NG24. London: NICE; 2015 (updated 2026).
Bullock MR, Chesnut R, Ghajar J, et al. Surgical management of acute subdural hematomas. Neurosurgery. 2006;58(3 Suppl):S16-S24.
Hutchinson PJ, Adams H, Mohan M, et al. Decompressive Craniectomy versus Craniotomy for Acute Subdural Hematoma. N Engl J Med. 2023;388(24):2219-2229.

start.text: A 76-year-old man who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation fell down the stairs at home with a brief loss of consciousness. In the emergency department his GCS is 14, and he has vomited twice.

ct.text: When should he have a head CT?

options.label: Within 8 hours of the injury, since his GCS is 14
options.feedback: NICE NG232: scan within 1 hour of identifying any of these: GCS 12 or less at first assessment, GCS below 15 at 2 hours, suspected open, depressed, or basal skull fracture, a post-traumatic seizure, a focal deficit, or more than one episode of vomiting. He has vomited twice.

options.label: Within 1 hour
options.feedback: NICE NG232: more than one episode of vomiting after a head injury is an indication for CT within 1 hour. Anticoagulant use alone would warrant considering a CT within 8 hours, and CT, not skull X-ray or MRI, is the primary investigation.

options.label: Skull X-ray first; CT only if there is a fracture
options.feedback: NICE NG232: CT is the primary investigation for clinically important brain injury, and plain skull X-rays should not be used to diagnose it. His two episodes of vomiting mean CT within 1 hour.

reverse.text: CT shows an acute left subdural hematoma. His INR is 3.2. First step while neurosurgery reviews the scan?

options.label: Fresh frozen plasma until the INR is below 1.5
options.feedback: NICE NG24: do not offer fresh frozen plasma to reverse a vitamin K antagonist. Give immediate prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin reversal after a head injury with suspected intracranial hemorrhage.

options.label: Stop the warfarin and let the INR drift down
options.feedback: NICE NG24: offer immediate prothrombin complex concentrate to reverse warfarin in a head injury with suspected intracranial hemorrhage. Stopping warfarin alone does not reverse anticoagulation quickly.

options.label: Immediate prothrombin complex concentrate, then recheck the INR
options.feedback: NICE NG24: offer immediate prothrombin complex concentrate for emergency warfarin reversal after a head injury with suspected intracerebral hemorrhage. Monitor the INR to confirm reversal and consider further doses. NICE NG232 points to this guidance for traumatic intracranial hemorrhage.

large.text: The hematoma is 12 mm thick with a 7 mm midline shift. His GCS is 13. Plan?

options.label: Serial CT and observation, since he is not in a coma
options.feedback: Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines (2006): an acute subdural hematoma thicker than 10 mm or with more than 5 mm of midline shift should be evacuated regardless of GCS. His is 12 mm with a 7 mm shift.

options.label: Evacuate as soon as possible
options.feedback: Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines (2006): evacuate an acute subdural hematoma thicker than 10 mm or with more than 5 mm of midline shift regardless of GCS, and operate as soon as possible once surgery is indicated.

small.text: The hematoma is 5 mm thick with no midline shift. His GCS stays at 14, with equal pupils. Plan?

options.label: Nonoperative care with close neurological observation, after reversal
options.feedback: Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines (2006): he meets none of the criteria for evacuation. Those are thickness over 10 mm or midline shift over 5 mm, or, in coma (GCS below 9), a fall of 2 or more GCS points, asymmetric or fixed pupils, or ICP above 20 mm Hg. NICE NG232 lists new clinically important imaging abnormalities, and a GCS that has not returned to 15, among its criteria for hospital admission.

options.label: Emergency craniotomy because he is anticoagulated
options.feedback: Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines (2006): surgery is indicated for thickness over 10 mm or midline shift over 5 mm, or for a comatose patient who deteriorates, has pupil asymmetry, or has ICP above 20 mm Hg. A 5 mm hematoma without shift in an alert patient meets none of these; anticoagulation is reversed, not operated on.

deteriorates.text: The hematoma is 8 mm thick with a 4 mm shift, but in the resuscitation room his GCS falls to 7 and his left pupil dilates. Plan?

options.label: ICP monitor only, as the hematoma is under 10 mm
options.feedback: Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines (2006): a comatose patient (GCS below 9) with a hematoma under 10 mm and shift under 5 mm still needs evacuation if the GCS has fallen by 2 or more points or the pupils are asymmetric or fixed and dilated. He has both.

options.label: Emergency evacuation
options.feedback: Brain Trauma Foundation surgical guidelines (2006): in coma, evacuate a subdural hematoma under 10 mm with under 5 mm shift if the GCS fell by 2 or more points, the pupils are asymmetric or fixed and dilated, or ICP exceeds 20 mm Hg. All comatose patients with acute subdural hematoma should have ICP monitoring.

technique.text: He goes to theatre. The 2006 guidelines advise craniotomy with or without bone flap removal and duraplasty in comatose patients. In RESCUE-ASDH, 12-month outcomes after craniotomy and decompressive craniectomy were similar (death 30.2% vs 32.2%). Craniotomy needed more further cranial surgery within 2 weeks (14.6% vs 6.9%), and craniectomy had more wound complications (12.2% vs 3.9%).

fail_delay.text: Diagnostic Delay: Head CT not done within the hour.

fail_undertreat.text: Complication: Brain herniation from an unevacuated hematoma.

fail_overtreat.text: Guideline Deviation: Craniotomy without a surgical indication.

success.text: Case Complete: Anticoagulation reversed and hematoma managed to criteria.
